Title: The Storyteller
Content: The leaves had fallen from `text(every tree)` except the oaks on the high ridges standing tall above the grassland. The last of the geese were veeing up to fly south as morning frost sparkled on the needles of the red pine. `text(Winter)` crept toward the plains, so the time had come for Red Bird the storyteller and her people to make the long trek into the hills, where they would be sheltered during the freezing `text(winter months)`. As final preparations for moving ensued, the wind turned cold and began blowing from the east. `text(Winter)` was on its way.

On the `text(second day)` of the journey, `text(winter)` warned them it was coming. Dark, rolling clouds crowded the sky. Gusts of wind laid the grasses flat and snarled through the branches of trees. The elders talked among themselves. The `text(winter)` lodges were still `text(ten)` grueling `text(days)` ahead on foot. Parents urged the children to hurry along. The chief could feel `text(winter)` on his heels and feared it would overtake his people. He set a brisk pace but slowed when it became too difficult for some. `text(One)` person suggested they break into groups, leaving `text(three)` or `text(four)` leaders behind to help the very old and the very young.
“We'll leave no one behind. It will be safest for all of us if we stay together,” the chief reasoned. “We must all help each other, support each other.”

No matter how fast they walked, `text(winter)` walked faster. On the `text(fourth day)`, it overtook them. The wind subsided and snow fell, turning later into sleet and forming piles around the bushes and clumps of grass. The path became slippery and muddy. `text(Winter)` hung above them, dark and threatening, and rose up, white and cold in the growing snow.

Everyone was drenched and drowsy by the time they made camp. `text(Each family)` made its shelter and huddled around a small fire. They exchanged looks, but no one complained about their ordeal. The wind picked up again just before morning. By the time the procession started, the wind had become a gale, and the snow blocked the view in all directions. `text(Winter)` hemmed them in. The group made little progress, and by `text(noon)` the snow had climbed to their knees. The elders decided it would be best to wait out the storm. Perhaps `text(winter)` would pass over soon enough.

“Tonight we'll stay together in `text(one)` shelter,” the chief decided. “We'll be safest if we huddle together, `text(each person)` keeping his or her neighbors warm. It will be difficult finding firewood, so we will work together to fuel `text(one)` fire.”

A large pine had been blown over and was caught between `text(two)` neighboring trees. The women cut its limbs to use as the frame for the shelter. They propped the limbs against the trunk and covered them with hides. The hides were in turn covered with pine boughs to seal the cracks and hold the walls in place. The children removed the snow from the floor of the makeshift shelter. The men spread out, searching for firewood, looking up for low-hanging dry limbs. By the time the last person returned, the snow was waist deep and drifting, and the wind had turned colder.

The people spent `text(two nights)` in the shelter while `text(winter)` `ultext(assailed)` them from all sides, dumping `text(four feet)` of snow and blowing drifts `text(twice)` that high in places. Though they tried valiantly, the people could gather very little firewood. On the `text(third night)`, the temperature plummeted. `text(Winter)` was going to freeze them out. Only a tiny flame flickered weak sparks of light. `text(Winter)` had trapped them and taken their hope.

But Red Bird had not given up. As the fire exhausted into a `text(single)` stream of smoke, Red Bird sang. Everyone knew the traditional song-it told of the way the sun had been placed in the sky and how it warmed the earth so that life sprang forth. When the song ended, Red Bird fought `text(winter)` with her words. She wove stories of `text(summer days)` when the sun was so bright it singed the tips of the cornstalks. She spoke of warm red rocks radiating heat and of the animals who took shelter in shaded places. With her words she pushed away `text(winter)` and carried her listeners through a desert where even the cactus bowed down in the heat. Her verbal tapestry wrapped around everyone inside the shelter and kept them warm. Despite her exhaustion and the bone-chilling cold, Red Bird fought `text(winter)` through the night, causing the imagination of her listeners to glow in the warmth of her descriptions. Red Bird spoke so beautifully and so bravely that nature listened. Sunshine greeted them in the morning. Red Bird fell silent. She was exhausted, but she had prevailed over `text(winter)` and saved her people.

A `text(day)` later, they continued their journey, carrying Red Bird, tired from her `text(night)` of battling `text(winter)`. Red Bird recovered and lived to tell many more stories, but none as important as the fires she created during the `ultext(arduous)` `text(winter nights)`.
